Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls this restriction weak; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects it."}, {"id": "96:5/q02/p3", "position": "Muhammad.", "reasons": "The reading cites 4:113. {"id": "96:5/q03", "question": "By what means does God teach unknown knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether learning is confined to writing or includes oral, rational, revealed and inspired routes.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q03/p1", "position": "By the pen and writing, which transmit knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says books carry learning across peoples and generations; Asad adds cultures and cumulative experience."}, {"id": "96:5/q03/p2", "position": "Through faculties, signs, reasoning, oral teaching, revelation and direct inspiration as well as writing.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī cites intuition, rational evidence, angels and messengers. Bayḍāwī cites faculties, signs and revealed verses. Biqāʿī includes uncaused insight and inference through premises and middle terms; Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes written, oral and intellectual routes. {"id": "96:5/q04", "question": "How is this teaching clause constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "The notes give different clause and predicate analyses.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q04/p1", "position": "'Taught' takes two objects.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās states the verb's transitivity."}, {"id": "96:5/q04/p2", "position": "The clause is the predicate of 'your Lord is most generous'; intervening words are parenthetical.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this parsing."}, {"id": "96:5/q04/p3", "position": "It is a fresh explanatory statement; this or 'who taught by the pen' may be predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's fuller discussion allows either predicate."}, {"id": "96:5/q04/p4", "position": "It parallels the earlier create/create-human pair.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the same grammatical analyses apply."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q05", "question": "How does this clause relate to 'who taught by the pen'?", "turns_on": "Whether it specifies the pen clause or adds further teaching.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q05/p1", "position": "It explains and specifies the pen teaching.", "reasons": "Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm says the prior object is omitted and supplied here, and repetition emphasizes teaching; Rāzī reports this. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees broader generic teaching."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q06", "question": "What explanatory reading explicitly mentions script?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q06/p1", "position": "Ibn al-Zubayr reads 'taught script by the pen'.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Ālūsī cite الذي علم الخط بالقلم; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports a similar Ibn ʿAbbās gloss, which Abū Ḥayyān calls explanatory."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q07", "question": "What does the wording of this clause emphasize?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q07/p1", "position": "Prior ignorance and unspecified knowledge stress God's power and generosity.", "reasons": "Al-Irshād says the omitted first object and stated prior ignorance hint at knowledge beyond human comprehension for Muhammad. Bursawī includes universal, particular, manifest and hidden knowledge."}, {"id": "96:5/q07/p2", "position": "Repeating 'taught' emphasizes and explains the pen clause.", "reasons": "Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm notes the repetition."}, {"id": "96:5/q07/p3", "position": "Knowledge follows a prior state of ignorance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says inability to read need not prevent later learning."}, {"id": "96:5/q07/p4", "position": "Repeated 'human' creates paronomasia.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī says the first denotes the species, the second Adam, a literate person or Idris, and the third Abū Jahl."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q08", "question": "How does the verse answer Muhammad's inability to read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q08/p1", "position": "God can teach him Qur'anic recitation directly despite his inability to write.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the verse answers 'I cannot read', by dictation, instruction or inspiration as God taught Adam names without literacy; with or without the hadith it reassures him. Biqāʿī says he will surpass writers; Ālūsī says God strengthens retention and proclamation."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q09", "question": "What does divine teaching show about God and humanity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q09/p1", "position": "It shows generosity, lordship and wisdom, raising humanity from ignorance to knowledge.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī and Nasafī contrast darkness and light. Ibn Kathīr calls these first verses mercy and blessing. Bayḍāwī and Biqāʿī describe a rise from lowest to highest, rational proof then transmitted or sensory knowledge. Al-Malawī argues knowledge is noblest since it follows 'most generous'. Ṭabrisī says knowledge comes from a knower. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'most generous' intensifies generosity rather than comparing God with another; divine gifts begin with creation and sustenance."}, {"id": "96:5/q09/p2", "position": "Knowledge dignifies humanity and distinguished Adam from the angels.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr distinguishes mental, verbal and written knowledge; writing entails the other two but not conversely. Biqāʿī notes generosity of teachers; Kuryolu says knowledge distinguishes people from other living things, citing 2:31."}, {"id": "96:5/q09/p3", "position": "God is the source of all human knowledge and discovery.", "reasons": "Qutb includes existence, life and self. Ibn ʿĀshūr says lordship implies existence and oneness, teaching and creation divine acts, and 'most generous' perfection."}, {"id": "96:5/q09/p4", "position": "Divinely granted knowledge can protect from self-assertion and transgression.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says the Prophet received knowledge before being established in abiding, guarding against a claim to independent perfection."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q10", "question": "Why is writing singled out in this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q10/p1", "position": "It preserves and transmits knowledge, wisdom, reports and revelation, sustaining religious and worldly life.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī and Nasafī say affairs fail without writing. Qatāda says knowledge sustains religion and livelihood. Biqāʿī extends benefits to both worlds. Ālūsī calls pen and script a sign of wisdom and cites poems about their reach. Asad stresses cumulative learning; Kuryolu includes computers and information exchange."}, {"id": "96:5/q10/p2", "position": "It encourages recording revelation and literacy.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says Muhammad appointed scribes from the start; his remaining unlettered completes the miracle, citing 29:48. Elmalılı says he dictated and relied on God's promise not to forget in 87:6."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q11", "question": "Who first learned or introduced writing, and how did scripts spread?", "turns_on": "Reports differ about first writers and the route of writing to Arabia.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q11/p1", "position": "Writing was divinely taught; Adam and other prophets may have learned it.", "reasons": "Zarkashī cites pen teaching and 68:1; Ibn Fāris places letters among the names taught Adam. {"id": "96:5/q13", "question": "Can acting on known knowledge bring further divine knowledge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q13/p1", "position": "Whoever acts on what he knows will receive knowledge he did not know.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits this maxim at adjacent verse locations; Suyūṭī cites it as a hadith on inspired knowledge."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q14", "question": "How much of al-ʿAlaq was the first revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the first revelation was only verses 1–5 or the whole surah.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q14/p1", "position": "The first five verses, ending here, came first; the rest came later.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha's Bukhārī and Muslim accounts recite through this verse; Zarkashī calls Bukhārī's shorter quotation abridged. {"id": "96:5/q15", "question": "Where and when did the teaching revelation arrive?", "turns_on": "Reports locate it differently.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q15/p1", "position": "At Hira during Muhammad's retreat.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha says truthful dreams and repeated seclusion with Khadīja's provisions preceded it. {"id": "96:5/q16", "question": "How did Gabriel convey the opening revelation?", "turns_on": "Accounts mention embraces, an inscribed cloth, or a chest opening.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q16/p1", "position": "He commanded Muhammad to read, pressed him three times, and recited the verses.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha has Muhammad answer 'I cannot read' and return trembling. {"id": "96:5/q17", "question": "What followed Muhammad's receipt of the opening verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q17/p1", "position": "Khadīja comforted him by citing his virtues.", "reasons": "Accounts name kinship, truth, hospitality, care for the needy and help in adversity; details vary. {"id": "96:5/q18", "question": "What revelations followed the opening passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q18/p1", "position": "Nūn and the Pen, al-Muddaththir and al-Ḍuḥā are listed after Iqraʾ.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha names these; Mujāhid adds Nūn and the Pen next. {"id": "96:5/q19", "question": "What is the surah's classification, verse count and reported virtue?", "turns_on": "The verse counts differ.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q19/p1", "position": "It is Meccan and has seventeen verses.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this count."}, {"id": "96:5/q19/p2", "position": "It is Meccan and has nineteen verses.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī gives this count."}, {"id": "96:5/q19/p3", "position": "Reciting it brings reward like reciting all shorter surahs.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī transmits the report."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q20", "question": "How do these verses connect to the surah's next turn and Qur'anic themes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q20/p1", "position": "Teaching calls for gratitude, yet the human transgresses.", "reasons": "Ālūsī supplies an implicit transition after verse 5. {"id": "96:5/q21", "question": "What did Muhammad's taḥannuth at Hira mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q21/p1", "position": "Secluded worship.", "reasons": "Bukhārī and Muslim gloss it as worship; ʿĀʾisha describes provisioning, Ibn Hishām a Ramadan retreat with feeding the poor and circumambulation after return."}, {"id": "96:5/q21/p2", "position": "A form of taḥannuf, meaning ḥanīfiyya.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām says Arabs replace th with f as in jadath/jadaf, citing Ruʾba; Abū ʿUbayda gives fam for thumma."}]}
{"id": "96:5/q22", "question": "What knowledge and method qualify a person to interpret the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "Directly taught unseen matters differ from disciplined inference and ungrounded opinion.", "positions": [{"id": "96:5/q22/p1", "position": "Some unseen and ambiguous passages require direct divine teaching.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha says Muhammad explained only what Gabriel taught; Ibn ʿAṭiyya limits that to unseen matters. Ibn ʿAṭiyya targets disregard of precedent and grammar or legal theory, while trained linguists and jurists may reason; early scholars either abstained or preserved tafsīr. Suyūṭī requires rhetoric, readings, theology, law, occasions, abrogation, fiqh and hadith; these sciences are an endless ocean."}, {"id": "96:5/q22/p3", "position": "ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās were leading early tafsīr authorities.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya ranks ʿAlī first, Ibn ʿAbbās next, then Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr; Ibn ʿAbbās learned from ʿAlī and was praised by ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; the Prophet prayed for his understanding."}]}

{"id": "96:6/q01", "question": "What does kallā do here?", "turns_on": "Whether a rebuke has an implicit or subsequent target, or the particle affirms or opens a new statement.", "positions": [{"id": "96:6/q01/p1", "position": "It rebukes or restrains transgression and ingratitude toward God's favors.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ calls it repudiation; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī supply the implicit object from God's preceding favors. Ibn ʿĀshūr instead points forward to the man prohibiting prayer and cites an opening negative oath of Imruʾ al-Qays. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ points to the following warning; Samarrāʾī notes kallā's concentration in the Qurʾān's second part and its fit with Meccan judgment themes."}, {"id": "96:6/q01/p2", "position": "It affirms the following statement: 'indeed' or 'truly'.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says neither side provides an object for repudiation and compares 74:32; al-Qurṭubī says no prior statement calls for a literal 'no'. Elmalılı reports this reading as keeping the address to the Prophet. Samarrāʾī explicitly reads ḥaqqan."}, {"id": "96:6/q01/p3", "position": "It means 'except'.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī compares 78:4 (kallā sawfa yaʿlamūn)."}, {"id": "96:6/q01/p4", "position": "It opens a new statement with the force of 'behold'.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim adduces Gabriel's first five verses, the pause after 96:5, and the later opening at 96:6; Ibn Hishām likewise treats it as a new opening, challenging a rebuke-only reading."}, {"id": "96:6/q01/p5", "position": "It corrects the human's failure to recognize God's creation and teaching.", "reasons": "Muqātil says wealth diverts the human from recognizing creation from a clot and teaching after ignorance."}, {"id": "96:6/q01/p6", "position": "It warns the Prophet not to cease repeating the command to read.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers continuity with the opening address to Muhammad; Abū Jahl exemplifies the self-sufficient transgressor against whom reading must continue."}]}
{"id": "96:6/q02", "question": "Who is al-insān here?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular denotes the immediate historical offender or humanity as a class despite that occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "96:6/q02/p1", "position": "Humanity generally, with Abu Jahl a prominent instance.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī prefers the surface context of creation, blessings and return to judgment (96:2, 96:8); al-Ālūsī allows a later Abu Jahl occasion without narrowing the noun; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the generic covers most people of that time except those restrained by religion or character. Kur'an Yolu extends it to every age."}, {"id": "96:6/q02/p2", "position": "Abu Jahl ibn Hishām in particular.", "reasons": "Muqātil links his growing wealth to better clothes, mounts, food and drink; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds his large council, hostility to Muhammad and ban on mosque prayer. Al-Rāzī says most exegetes identify him, although he prefers the generic sense. Al-Suyūṭī identifies this as the third al-insān, contrasting earlier occurrences."}]}
{"id": "96:6/q03", "question": "What does yaṭghā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression describes moral boundary crossing, social ascent, or a possible Semitic parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "96:6/q03/p1", "position": "To exceed proper bounds in disobedience, arrogance, rebellion or tyranny.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara and Corpus Coranicum derive the moral sense from water overflowing at 69:11; Corpus Coranicum also cites 69:5, 53:17 and early Meccan human uses including 91:11 and 79:17. Al-Ālūsī includes following desire; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses pride when secure enough to overstep others; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ invokes despots. The shades 'disobey', 'arrogance', and 'insolence' differ in wording but share this boundary crossing."}, {"id": "96:6/q03/p2", "position": "To rise from one rank or social level to another.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī gives rank advancement; al-Kalbī specifies clothing, food and similar signs of status.
